items.text: SEASON 12 · EPISODE 4 · DRAFT · CASE-063  Fenwright Group · month five · Pim (junior technician, APAC rota), Maya (asleep, eight hours away), Galen (on leave) · Level L6 · Mastery support (reference only — choose the tool and say why)  For most of this episode you are not Maya. It's eleven in the morning in Singapore and three at headquarters, the APAC all-hands is live in twelve offices — and the person on the rota is Pim.  ⚑ RV-187: the event is the producer's, the network its owner's, the runbooks the team's. RV-188: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock — and some depend on your loadout.

items.title: The Runbook Worked
items.stakes: Twelve APAC offices lose the all-hands stream. It's three in the morning where the architect is.
items.reward: The stream back without waking anyone — and every runbook pointing at roles.

objectives.text: Decide what makes the failover step reliable

items.sub: Month five · 11:10 a.m. Singapore · 3:10 a.m. at headquarters

items.alt: The Singapore office's event room: the big screen tiled with offices, the top two rows dark; Pim holds the runbook binder open, worried but steady.

bubbles.text: Twelve offices just lost the stream. Runbook seven. Step one: confirm the alert.

items.caption: Three in the morning where the architect is.

lines.text: Twelve offices just lost the stream. Runbook seven.
Step one: confirm the alert. Okay. Okay.

items.prompt: You're Pim. 11:12: the stream-health alert is confirmed — twelve offices dark. What now?
items.risk: An all-hands lost — or an architect who can never sleep.
timeout: The producer goes to audio-only by phone.

hints.text: What's the first step written down — and who wrote it for exactly this?

options.label: Call Maya — she designed it
options.result: 03:12 at headquarters. She answers, half asleep, and asks what the runbook says.
options.consequence: Wakes the author to read her own runbook.

options.label: Follow RB-07 step by step: encoder status, uplink, platform — then the switch to the backup encoder path, and verify at two remote offices
options.result: Encoder not responding; uplink healthy; backup path at 11:18; picture and captions confirmed in Manila and Perth at 11:19.

options.label: Restart the encoder and hope
options.result: Four minutes of reboot. It crashes again at 11:20.

options.label: Tell the producer to stop the all-hands
options.result: Two thousand people told to go back to work.
options.consequence: Ends the event instead of restoring it.

items.title: Nine minutes.
items.body: Down at 11:10, alert at 11:12, diagnosed at 11:15, restored on the backup path at 11:19: T = 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 minutes, against a target of fifteen. Maya's review the next morning finds out why it went so smoothly: in March, the juniors ran RB-07 cold in a drill, with its author watching and not allowed to help. They found three wrong steps — an old status page, a missing login for the backup, no remote office to check. All three were fixed within a week. Every one of them was used last night.
items.label: Test: what the drill saved — and which stage the backup shortened.

items.alt: A timeline of the all-hands from 11:05 to 11:25: the stream green until 11:10, red for nine minutes, then blue on the backup; Pim's lane shows detect (2 min), diagnose (3 min), restore (4 min); a dashed 15-minute target box. Step 9 named Galen, on leave; Pim rang the APAC duty manager.
items.caption: Nine minutes.

items.title: ‘3 steps wrong · fixed by 21 Mar’
items.body: The March drill notes, in Noor's handwriting: ‘Juniors ran RB-07 cold. Step 2 pointed at the old encoder page. Step 4 missed the backup's login. Step 5 had no remote office to check. Fixed by the 21st.’ Every one of those steps worked last night.

items.sub: Mastery · the skill behind this chapter

items.prompt: Next morning. The backup encoder path saved the event. How does it stay a four-minute step?
items.risk: A backup that fails the day it's needed.
timeout: The backup gets its first test the next time the primary fails.

hints.text: What turns a backup into a step you can trust?

items.note: Draft decision (DR-S12E04). Option B needs Redundancy at LIMITED or better.

options.label: Leave it as it is — it worked
options.result: In October the backup's licence lapses. Nobody notices until it's needed.

options.label: Keep the backup path warm — running, licensed, monitored — and switch a real event to it once a month, with the runbook's step 4 pointing at it
options.result: The first monthly test finds nothing wrong. The second finds an expired certificate a month before it would have mattered.
options.consequence: Warm and tested beats spare and hopeful.

options.label: Keep a spare encoder in the cupboard, ready to set up if the primary fails
options.result: Setting it up is a forty-minute project at 3 a.m.
options.consequence: The best you can do without a second warm path — slower, but a plan.

options.label: Buy a better primary encoder
options.result: A better single point of failure.

items.title: The checklist that saved a bomber
items.body: In 1935, the prototype of a large new four-engine bomber crashed on a test flight: the experienced pilot had forgotten to release a lock on the controls. The aircraft was judged ‘too much airplane for one man to fly’. The answer wasn't a better pilot. It was a short checklist, read at every take-off — and the idea spread through aviation. Expertise forgets steps; a written list, used every time, doesn't.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #115 · AVERY'S LENS  A runbook is proven by the people who'll use it  The test of a runbook isn't whether its author can follow it — it's whether a junior can, at three in the morning, with the author asleep. Drill it with them; name roles, not people.  A stream failed in the middle of a regional all-hands. A junior restored it in nine minutes from a runbook — and nobody woke the architect.

items.title: Step nine.
items.body: The log shows the one step that didn't work. Step nine: ‘Call Galen to approve failback to the primary.’ Galen was on leave, somewhere over the Atlantic. Pim didn't fail back without approval — he stayed on the backup, which was safe, and rang the APAC duty manager from the rota sheet on the office wall. Exactly right, and nowhere in the runbook. Maya checks the other thirteen runbooks. Nine of fourteen name a person somewhere; Galen's name is in five.
items.label: Test: how many runbooks name a person — and what Pim did instead.

items.prompt: How do the runbooks keep working after you've gone?
items.risk: A runbook that stops at a name.
timeout: Galen's name stays in five runbooks.

hints.text: What stays true when every person in the runbook is on leave?

options.label: Change step nine to Galen's deputy
options.result: The deputy goes on leave in August.
options.consequence: A different name is still a name.

options.label: Every call in every runbook goes to a role on the rota; the runbooks are drilled every quarter by the juniors who'll run them; findings fixed within a week, owned by the team lead
options.result: Galen reads his own name out of five runbooks. Next drill: EMEA, month eight — Noor runs it, Maya only watches.
options.consequence: Roles, drills, fixes — without the author.

options.label: Add Maya's number as a last resort to every runbook
options.result: Maya leaves in seven months. Her number doesn't.
options.consequence: Makes the author the fallback forever.

options.label: Rewrite all the runbooks yourself, properly this time
options.result: Beautiful runbooks nobody else has ever run.

items.alt: The same timeline, annotated after the review: nine minutes, six inside the target; every runbook call now goes to a role on the rota, drilled every quarter by juniors; nobody called the architect.
items.caption: Roles, not names.

bubbles.text: Five runbooks with my name in. I'm flattered and horrified.
‘APAC on-call engineer.’ That's me this week. It's somebody else next week. That's the point.

items.prompt: I nearly rang you at step nine. It was three in the morning for you.

options.label: “Ringing the duty manager was exactly right. And step nine is my fault — it had a name in it. Help me fix all of them?”
options.reply: All of them. Galen's name is in five.

options.label: “Next time, just fail back.”
options.reply: Without approval? In the middle of an all-hands?

bubbles.text: Halfway through your year. If you left tomorrow, what would break?
Give me a week and I'll give you a number.

items.teaser: the rota on the Singapore office wall
items.title: ‘APAC duty manager · this week’
items.body: A laminated sheet on the office wall: ‘APAC duty manager — this week’ and a phone number. Nobody had put it in the runbook. Pim had walked past it every day for three months.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  A runbook works at 3 a.m. when the people who'll use it have already run it: drill it with juniors while its author watches, fix what they find within a week, and keep every backup path warm and tested so failover is a step, not a project. Add up the restore — detect, diagnose, restore (T = Σ stages) — and design each stage. Name roles on a rota, never people: the best sign a runbook works is that nobody needed its author.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Whose name is in your runbooks — and where are they tonight?
